Situation1: Your friend has misunderstood the tone of your text message and replied sounding hurt. You need to call them right now to explain.
Expectation2: Perform assigned physical tasks and material handling efficiently.
Situation2: A carpenter is waiting for you to bring them the next load of lumber so they can continue their work without interruption.
Story:
My phone buzzes in my pocket just as I’m hoisting a heavy plank onto my shoulder. I glance at the screen and see a message from Sam, my best friend. His words sting: “Didn’t know you felt that way.” My heart sinks. He’s misunderstood my last text, and I can tell he’s hurt. I know I should call him right now, clear things up before the misunderstanding festers. That’s what friends do—communicate, fix things before they break.

But the foreman’s voice cuts through my thoughts. “Hey! The carpenter’s waiting! We need that lumber, now!” I see the carpenter tapping his foot, tools in hand, looking straight at me. If I don’t get this load over, the whole crew will be held up, and I’ll be the reason for the delay. My hands tighten on the wood, sweat prickling my brow—not just from the heat, but from the pressure squeezing me from both sides. I can’t be in two places at once. My friend needs me, but so does my team. I stand there, torn, the phone buzzing again in my pocket, the weight of the lumber digging into my shoulder.
